column1: Regenerative cotton farming package using enriched biochar from cotton stalks combined with bokashi and jeevamrit, delivered through a train-the-trainer model to boost yields, soil carbon, and farmer incomes in Cameroon.

column5: The innovation rejuvenates soil health by producing biochar from cotton stalks and enriching it with bokashi (microorganism source) and jeevamrit (microbial “food”). The porous biochar structure retains water and nutrients; combined amendments stimulate microbial activity, improve fertility, and can neutralize acidic soils. Delivery uses a cascade model: 60 agricultural advisors train 3,000 lead farmers, who demonstrate and train ~42,000 farmers via farmer field schools. Early outputs include thousands trained, hundreds of trial plots, >200 t of biochar produced, and preliminary yield gains with an average yield increase of around 40% across participating farmers (from ~1.356 t/ha to ~2.956 t/ha on trial plots). Soil carbon increases are being measured; potential sequestration is ~3 t CO?-eq/ha/yr.
column6: Cotton stalks that are normally burned after harvest are collected and converted into biochar using simple, low-cost pyrolysis methods. The biochar is then combined with microbial soil amendments such as bokashi or jeevamrit to enhance soil biological activity. Farmers apply this mixture to their cotton fields, where the porous structure of biochar improves soil moisture retention, nutrient availability, and soil structure. As soil health improves, cotton yields increase while the need for chemical inputs such as fertilizers and insecticides decreases. column10: Status Quo. In Cameroon’s cotton sector, post?harvest residues are typically burned in the field to control pests. The scaling assessment notes that the biochar used in this project comes from cotton stalks that are normally burnt by farmers in the fields; burning releases additional CO?, whereas converting the stalks to biochar retains the carbon. These stalks therefore represent a biomass resource that is currently wasted and whose combustion deprives soils of organic matter. Research on crop?residue management shows that burning wet biomass produces large quantities of CO? and fine particulate matter. Although the project documents focus on biochar, agronomic studies have highlighted that intensive use of synthetic fertilisers often leads to soil degradation and poor nutrient?use efficiency, only 30–50 % of applied nutrients are taken up, with the remainder lost to the environment, and that fertiliser expenses are a substantial cost component in crop production. | Alternatives & Competitive Position. Conventional organic amendments such as compost improve fertility but lack the long?term structural benefits of biochar. The scaling document describe biochar as a porous product that increases water?storage capacity, enabling soils to absorb more rainfall and neutralise acidity. The project’s regenerative package combines biochar derived from cotton stalks with Bokashi (a source of microorganisms) and Jeevamrit (a nutrient?rich microbial inoculant); together these three supplements create a balanced and dynamic soil ecosystem. Preliminary field results in Cameroon support this synergy: on trial plots, average seed?cotton yields rose from 1.356 t?ha?¹ in 2023 to 2.956 t?ha?¹ in 2024/25, an approximate 100 % increase. Across farmers participating in the programme, the average cotton yield increase is approximately 40 %. Because biochar’s carbon matrix is stable, it can sequester about 3 t CO??eq per hectare per year, offering a climate benefit absent from compost?only systems. By turning a waste product into a valuable amendment and combining it with potent microbial inoculants, this innovation provides a circular, climate?positive alternative to residue burning or compost alone. Adoption challenges such as labour and knowledge are mitigated through a train?the?trainer cascade: 60 agricultural advisors train 3 000 lead farmers, who in turn train 42 000 farmers via farmer field schools, keeping per?farmer costs low and ensuring wide dissemination.
column11: For a scaling investment of €25 per farmer, the project delivers a high cost-benefit ratio. Additionally, the method reduces costs by lowering the need for chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

column22: Transforming cotton stalks into biochar and integrating it with bokashi or jeevamrit enhances soil structure, moisture, and nutrient retention while neutralizing acidity. Improved soil health leads to higher and more stable cotton yields, reducing residue burning and fertilizer dependence. In addition, as old cotton stalks are cut down and processed into biochar, this kills the larvae that normally survives the dry season on the stalks and consequently reducing the amount of insecticides and the costs for chemicals.These agronomic gains translate into higher incomes and greater resilience for farming households. These improvements contribute to an average cotton yield increase of around 40%, alongside reduced input costs. As residue burning declines, long-term soil-carbon sequestration increases, contributing to climate mitigation. Through advisor and lead-farmer training, peer learning, and local demonstrations, these regenerative practices become embedded within farming systems, reinforcing a sustainable cycle of soil restoration, productivity, and environmental recovery.
